e.etymology: A respelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Katherine, which reached Ireland through Old French Cateline. Katherine is from Greek Aikaterine, long linked with katharos, pure.
A pet form of Clementine, and sometimes of Clement, from Latin clemens, merciful or gentle. It was given as a full name in the US in the late 1800s.
A respelling of Jeremy, the medieval English form of Jeremiah, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, the Lord will exalt.
The Italian form of Guy, from the Germanic name Wido, probably a short form of names beginning with widu, wood or forest.

assoc.t: American slang stereotype of a flashy Italian-American man

e.note: In American slang guido is a mocking, often offensive label for a flashy Italian-American man.

e.etymology: A variant of Susan, shortened from Susanna and Susanne, which go back to Hebrew Shoshannah, lily.
A respelling of Christina, from Latin Christiana, a Christian woman, built on the Greek title Christos, anointed one.
A turn-of-the-century American name close in sound to Delores, the English spelling of Spanish Dolores.
A spelling of Mandy, the pet form of Amanda, from Latin amanda, she who should be loved.
An early 1900s American name that reads as Vera with the La- prefix, in the same family as Laverne and Lavern.
A phonetic American spelling of Juanita, the Spanish pet form of Juana, the feminine of Juan (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious.
A spelling of Adrienne, the French feminine of Adrien (Adrian), from Latin Hadrianus, a man from Hadria, the town that also named the Adriatic Sea.

e.meaning: flax farm or lime tree settlement
e.etymology: An English surname from the many places called Linton, Old English tun (settlement) joined to either lin (flax) or lind (lime tree).
A pet form of Keziah, one of Job's daughters, whose Hebrew name means cassia. It leapt into use in 1977 after Kizzy in Alex Haley's Roots, where the name is explained as Mandinka for stay put.

assoc.t: Kizzy, Kunta Kinte's daughter in Roots

e.etymology: The German sports car marque, named for its founder Ferdinand Porsche, taken up as an American girls' name in the 1980s. It sounds like Portia and is often a respelling of it.

assoc.t: Porsche, the German sports car maker

e.note: Most people will think of the sports car first.

e.etymology: An American spelling of Olivia, from Latin oliva, olive or olive branch, a name Shakespeare made popular with Twelfth Night.
An English surname from places named in Old English for a birch wood or clearing. In Ireland Bartley is also a long-standing everyday form of Bartholomew.
A short form of Cherilyn (Cheryl plus -lyn), made a name of its own by the singer Cher, born Cherilyn Sarkisian. It also matches French cher, dear.

assoc.t: Cher, pop singer and Oscar-winning actress
Cher Horowitz, the heroine of the film Clueless

e.etymology: A mid-century American name that joins Jerry to the -yl ending of Daryl and Cheryl. It has been given to both boys and girls.
From the Scots word laddie, a boy or young man. Among Czech and Slovak Americans it was also the usual English pet form of Ladislav, a form of Vladislav.
Coined by the Scottish poet James Macpherson for his Ossian poems of the 1760s, from Gaelic mala-mhin, smooth brow. The Argentine name for the Falklands, Las Malvinas, is unrelated.
The German form of Bernard, from Old High German bero (bear) and hart (hard, strong).
A respelling of Bernard, also found as a French surname. Bernard joins the Germanic words for bear and for hard or strong, and came to England with the Normans.
A respelling of Sadie, the old pet form of Sarah, from Hebrew sarah, princess or noblewoman.
A form of Caspar or Jasper, the name tradition gives one of the three Magi, thought to come from a Persian word for treasurer. Gasper matches Slovene Gasper and anglicizes Italian Gaspare.
Vietnamese Tuan, written with a tone mark, is the Sino-Vietnamese reading of a Chinese character for handsome and talented. It came into US records with Vietnamese families after 1975.
Two names share this spelling. In the US around 1900 it was a form of Tommie, a pet form of Thomas that was also given to girls. In Japan Tomie, said toh-mee-eh, is a separate women's name.
namesakes: Tomie dePaola (author and illustrator of Strega Nona)

e.etymology: A variant of Sylvester, from Latin silvester, wooded or of the forest, from silva, wood. Saint Silvester's feast is December 31, so in German Silvester is also the word for New Year's Eve.
A mid-century American compound of Jeri, a short form of Geraldine, and Lynn.

An English place name and surname, Old English wine (friend, or the personal name Wine) plus thorp (village). It became a New England first name in honor of John Winthrop, founding governor of Massachusetts Bay.
